comparator.name: Earth, Climate and Technology
comparator.sourceNotes: This qualified academic-core comparison assesses the adopted 2026–2027 first- and second-year taught core (120 EC) and 30 EC of eligible minor study: 150 documented EC. The full degree has 180 EC. Excluded are the redesigned third-year Engineering Design Project (5 EC), EC&T programme elective (5 EC), Spatiotemporal Data Analysis (5 EC) and individual Bachelor Thesis Project (15 EC). Their detailed formation, entry and selection conditions and full-degree progression remain unverified. The known physics, transport and integrated field-engineering requirements within the assessed core remain explicit differences, rather than being removed to improve the comparison. Current programme24623(B-TA,56959) confirms the renamed English full-time Earth,Climate and Technology successor to Applied Earth Sciences; the adopted TER has no tracks. Complete current catalogue has25redesigned units120EC and6legacy third-year entries; legacy10ECthesis is not the new15ECthesis. FormalECTB110A/B map by exacttitle and4+4ECto guideECTB1110A/B. Retain the separately verified Sensing-first-sit4.3 before FieldProjectpreparation4.4 andfield4.6–4.8, conditional on actual successful assignments/exam completion, with no resit/concurrency waiver. AnnexArticle6 delegates entry to the guide; no old140/170ECthreshold is imported. Minor admission, non-overlap, coherence and prior approval rules remain applicable. Geology for Engineering also names a first-year prerequisite code absent from the current table; its equivalence or extra preparation remains unverified. This comparison assesses documented academic content and minor structure, not a certified progression route or unrestricted minor capacity.
components: Exploring the Grand Challenges: Data and Python
Exploring the Grand Challenges: Application and Skills

Required 4-EC field course. Expected preparation includes first-semester Earth and Climate System and Exploring the Grand Challenges, and participation in Surface, Water and Atmosphere and Geodata Fundamentals.
Expected preparation names ECTB1120A, absent from the adopted table, which lists ECTB1121A/B. Its current equivalence or any additional preparation remains unverified; no waiver is assumed.

Required 10-EC field campaign with named prerequisites. The first Sensing exam precedes preparation and fieldwork, conditional on actual successful completion; no late-resit or concurrency waiver is assumed.
30 EC of eligible non-overlapping minor study; positive BSA and any minor entry requirements apply. An outside-LDE, self-composed or foreign minor requires prior approval under the current rules.

core: Integrated Earth-system processes across subsurface, surface, water and atmosphere
Mathematics, physics, chemistry, geodata, sensing, modelling and uncertainty
Field investigation, engineering design, research and societal impact
adjacent: Subsurface resources, geothermal energy, storage and responsible extraction
Climate dynamics, environmental change, adaptation and resilience
Earth observation, spatial data and environmental monitoring
questions: How can subsurface resources and energy systems be developed responsibly?
How can field observations, sensors, satellite data and models reveal Earth and climate change?
How can technical Earth-system solutions address climate risk and environmental resilience?

alternatives.label: Earth systems, climate & quantitative inquiry
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate Earth processes and climate through geological fieldwork, geospatial observation, soil and aquifer characterization, geochemistry and mathematical inquiry. Combine numerical methods with physical energy-system study and environmental research. This broader geoscience response differs from Delft’s fuller mechanics, fluid/field physics and integrated field-engineering formation.
alternatives.concept: Investigate Earth processes and climate through geological fieldwork, geospatial observation, soil and aquifer characterization, geochemistry and mathematical inquiry. Combine numerical methods with physical energy-system study and environmental research. This broader geoscience response differs from Delft’s fuller mechanics, fluid/field physics and integrated field-engineering formation.
progression: Planned six-term offerings and every formal prerequisite pass. Physical-science foundations precede dependent observation/resource/energy study; Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods and selected signal/advanced calculus work. Guided partner research is taken in its sole planned first term with no formal prerequisite, and does not promise geological fieldwork or a thesis. Multivariable calculus is in the available final2029springterm, so mathematical sequencing differs from Delft.

alternatives.label: Climate, signals & geospatial data
alternatives.labelReason: Use Earth observation, spatial data, signal analysis and computation to investigate environmental change. Combine actual GIS and remote-sensing study with linear systems, numerical methods, machine learning and image processing, while retaining geological and climate foundations. Dedicated geoscience datasets, sensor deployment and Delft’s complete geophysical time-series formation are not guaranteed.
alternatives.concept: Use Earth observation, spatial data, signal analysis and computation to investigate environmental change. Combine actual GIS and remote-sensing study with linear systems, numerical methods, machine learning and image processing, while retaining geological and climate foundations. Dedicated geoscience datasets, sensor deployment and Delft’s complete geophysical time-series formation are not guaranteed.
progression: Planned six-term offerings and every formal prerequisite pass. Physical-science foundations precede dependent observation/resource/energy study; Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods and selected signal/advanced calculus work. Guided partner research is taken in its sole planned first term with no formal prerequisite, and does not promise geological fieldwork or a thesis. General computational projects are not guaranteed Earth-science applications.
alternatives.distinctness: A sustained signal/computational strand replaces the closest programme’s probability, physical-energy, remediation, water-management and advanced-calculus choices with linear systems, algorithms, machine learning, image processing and nature-based engineering. The difference is37.5ECeach way and has an independent data/sensing purpose.

alternatives.label: Subsurface resources, energy & responsibility
alternatives.labelReason: Study subsurface resources and the energy transition through geology, soils, geochemistry, field evidence and quantitative methods. Connect geothermal and storage questions with physical renewable-energy systems, recovery and remediation, life-cycle impacts and environmental justice. This is a broader resource-and-responsibility direction, without promising reservoir engineering or a complete extraction-design sequence.

alternatives.distinctness: Life-cycle assessment, nature-based engineering, linear systems and environmental justice replace the closest programme’s data-science, probability, water-management and advanced-calculus choices. Against the data direction, resource/energy, recovery, life-cycle and justice study replace generic machine learning, data science, algorithms and computer vision. Each comparison differs by30ECeach way for a coherent resource/energy priority.

trace: Sustainability Essentials I supplies physical, mathematical and systems foundations for studying linked environmental change.
Dynamic Earth directly examines structural geology, Earth history and environmental geology through laboratory and field work.
Introduction to Programming develops Python-based computational problem solving for environmental data and models.

Direct wave physics, observational methods, chemical analysis and materials stress/strain connect physical evidence to environmental and resource questions; sustainability-campaign work adds critical communication, not a general Earth-system modelling course.

Develops single-variable calculus, complex numbers, integration, differential equations and analytical/Mathematica dynamic-model investigation. These are substantive Earth-system mathematical foundations; vector/matrix methods belong to the separately selected Linear Algebra course rather than this course.
Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations applies geoscience to disasters, environmental change and adaptation.
Earth System Science Tools integrates Earth-system modelling, tracers, proxies and greenhouse-gas pathways.
Climate Change directly studies anthropogenic climate change, ocean acidification and climate adaptation.
Introduction to Data Science develops cleaning, visualisation and analysis of spatial and other datasets.
Probability & Statistics develops probability, distributions and parameter estimation for environmental evidence.

Direct ArcGIS geospatial analysis, spatial data representation and surface analysis with remote-sensing/spectral acquisition and image processing; an environmental case study applies these tools. No guaranteed drone deployment or advanced temporal geostatistics.

Direct soil properties, formation, quality, salinization and field/laboratory characterization; seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate soils/aquifers. Do not infer a full groundwater-flow or freshwater-resource course.
Living with Water examines flood protection, freshwater management, land subsidence and ecological consequences.
Computational & Numerical Methods develops numerical modelling, root finding and differential-equation methods.
Environmental Biogeochemistry uses geochemical modelling to analyse waters, minerals and element cycles.

Applied research process with a Zeeland sustainability partner: literature,question,investigation andfinalproduct/report. Subject and techniques depend on the project; no guaranteed geological fieldwork or international engineering design.
R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation applies environmental chemistry and laboratory methods to resource recovery and contamination.

Develops regression/classification, resampling, regularisation, trees, support-vector and unsupervised-learning methods with real-data projects. These are complementary methods for environmental/spatial analysis; a dedicated Earth-science dataset or project is not guaranteed.
Earth’s Resources provides advanced geoscience research on geothermal energy, subsurface carbon storage, nuclear-waste storage and responsible resource use.
Governance of Sustainability examines institutions and interests shaping climate adaptation and environmental action.
Renewable System Design develops technical and economic assessment of lower-carbon energy systems through an external-company project.
Linear Algebra supplies vector and matrix methods used in spatial modelling and data science.
Building with Nature examines ecosystem-based design, land reclamation and flood protection.
Algorithms & Data Structures develops efficient computational methods for large and complex datasets.

Specific complementary digital-image representation,filtering,segmentation,feature detection andrecognition usingPython/OpenCV; these computational techniques can support Earth observation,without claiming dedicated remote-sensing acquisition.
Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy evaluates environmental impacts of technologies and resource use across complete life cycles.

Direct continuous/discrete signal and linear-system methods, Fourier/Laplace/Z transforms,sampling,filtering andfeedback. Complements geophysical sensing; no guaranteed stochastic geoscience time-series or geological model.
Social Movements & Environmental Justice examines the justice, participation and conflict dimensions of resource extraction and environmental intervention.

Physical renewable-resource/yield calculations, conversion, storage/grids and actual Polysun/mini-grid work strengthen energy-system inquiry. No subsurface-extraction or full thermodynamics course is inferred.

The current official description supports multivariable calculus, differential equations, complex-valued functions and computer algebra. It strengthens mathematical Earth-science foundations within description-only limits; its late planned offering does not reproduce Delft’s sequence.
blocks: Both examine interactions among Earth spheres and use models to interpret climate/system processes. UCR’s actual description includes proxies, tracers and greenhouse-gas pathways; Delft’s paired foundation also gives a broader geology/physical-climate introduction.

The guide describes a combined Earth/climate subject for the two formal 4-EC parts. No second one-course equivalence is counted from that shared content; UCR geological and climate contributions also occur elsewhere.

Both address surface/water problems. UCR studies flooding, salinity, freshwater, subsidence and context-sensitive delta adaptation; Delft gives a more quantitative geomorphology, hydrology and atmospheric-process sequence.
The second part belongs to the combined surface/water/atmosphere course. No second UCR counterpart to its quantitative hydrological and boundary-layer/atmospheric scope is asserted.

Actual geological observation, measurement, rock/mineral identification, mapping, cross-sections and stratigraphic interpretation supply a genuine field-method relationship. Delft integrates more Earth spheres, sensors and poster work along the Meuse; the complete field formats differ.

UCR geology, shallow-subsurface characterization and resource research contribute relevant substance. A full counterpart to Delft’s basin evolution, multiscale heterogeneity and subsurface-engineering interpretation is not established.
UCR climate study supplies actual physical drivers and system/impact context. It does not reproduce the governing-equation and rotating-fluid treatment of atmospheric and ocean circulation.

Both study anthropogenic climate drivers, feedbacks, impacts and societal responses. Delft additionally requires guided climate-dataset/model-output evaluation; UCR’s course does not guarantee the same quantitative climate-analysis workflow.

Actual soil/shallow-aquifer sampling, laboratory characterization and seismic/electrical/electromagnetic surveys supply a substantive characterization-method contribution. Delft extends into deeper petrophysics, cone penetration, upscaling and engineering uncertainty.

UCR has actual geological fieldwork, geophysical soil surveys, Earth-observation projects and guided sustainability research. These do not reproduce Delft’s integrated three-week French field survey/application-driven engineering campaign; generic partner research is not used to fill this 10-EC requirement.

Both develop Python programming and computational problem solving. Delft integrates the code with Earth-system data and grand-challenge inquiry; UCR does not guarantee a geoscience programming project.
UCR physical-science foundations contain real mechanics/material and modelling work, but no full counterpart to Delft’s Newtonian particle/rigid-body and continuum-mechanics treatment is established.
Physical renewable-energy calculations are genuine UCR contributions. They do not establish Delft’s full heat/work, state-change, mixing and thermodynamic treatment.

Both cover multivariable calculus and differential equations. UCR’s official description supports this mathematical scope and computer algebra, without establishing every vector/multiple-integral topic or Delft’s first-year timing.

Probability, distributions, inference, parameter estimation and uncertainty form a direct statistical contribution. Delft also teaches physical sensing and geophysical/remote-sensing acquisition within its geodata workflow.

Actual model fitting, selection, validation and prediction in R/Python provide a substantive statistical-learning contribution in the data direction. Delft’s dedicated Earth-data/Python workflow differs and is not guaranteed by UCR projects.

Both develop quantitative Earth/environmental chemistry, including aqueous/mineral systems, equilibrium, redox and modelling. UCR provides advanced geochemical/laboratory inquiry; Delft gives a broader foundational thermodynamic/chemical sequence.

Both develop vectors, matrices, linear systems, transformations, eigenvalues, subspaces and projections. UCR adds actual least-squares/SVD and computer-algebra applications; institutional scope and timing differ.

Both teach signals, linear systems, convolution, Fourier methods, sampling and filtering. Delft additionally develops stochastic time-series/noise analysis and Earth-system applications; UCR supplies broader signal/system methods.
UCR has real wave, measurement and numerical-method contributions. No complete counterpart to Delft’s vector-calculus/PDE treatment of potential, diffusion and wave fields is asserted.
Actual soil/water, energy and numerical work contributes relevant applications, but does not establish a complete fluid-dynamics and heat/mass/momentum-conservation course.

Actual GIS spatial representation/analysis, georeferencing, surface analysis, remote-sensing foundations and image processing give a direct geospatial contribution. UCR uses ArcGIS Pro; Delft uses QGIS/Python with wider geophysical, stochastic and uncertainty methods.

Numerical systems/ODE algorithms, integration, root finding, error and stability are substantial modelling methods. Delft adds explicit geophysical PDE discretization, governing-equation workflows and high-performance computing that are not guaranteed here.
Both develop academic communication, integrity, teamwork and reflection. UCR adds civic/personal development; Delft embeds these skills in engineering and Earth-system challenges.

Both examine societal consequences, stakeholders, ethical choices and sustainability responses. UCR uses governance frameworks, stakeholder/expert inquiry and policy advice; Delft gives engineering decisions and impacts a specific setting.
Eligible non-overlapping 30-EC minor study remains uninstantiated. Positive BSA, individual minor entry/coherence and required prior approvals apply; no unrestricted or invented minor is shown.

notes.text: Delft provides fuller mechanics, thermodynamics, fluid and field physics, geophysical/time-series analysis, deeper subsurface engineering and an integrated international field-engineering campaign. UCR offers actual geology fieldwork, soil/geophysical surveys, geospatial analysis, geochemistry, mathematics and physical energy-system inquiry, with a broader environmental focus.

This is an academic-core comparison. The 150-EC table includes 120 EC of taught core and 30 EC of eligible minor study. The other 30 EC of required Delft design, elective, spatiotemporal and thesis formation are excluded. Each UCR program remains a complete 24-course, 180-EC plan; no extra independent research is counted within it. The optional 15-EC research shown separately is additional and does not replace Delft’s excluded thesis.

selection.assessment: Three independently supported broader core responses: quantitative Earth/climate inquiry, dedicated climate/signal/geospatial analysis, and resource/energy responsibility. Substantive mathematical/energy and signal improvements produce pairwise37.5/30/30ECdifferences; no threshold-only substitutions. Stop at three. No programme certifies Delft’s full engineering or required third-year formation.

acceptance.claim: Actual UCR geological field, Earth-system, geospatial, soil/geochemical and mathematical/physical-energy inquiry supports a broader comparison with the confirmed taught Earth, Climate and Technology core and two distinct related directions. Complete technical-physics, field-engineering and graduation equivalence are not claimed.
